summary.text: For primes \(p,q\) with different final digits and \(pq\le150\), at least one must divide \(d\): otherwise \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\), so some index \(i<pq\) makes \(a+id\) divisible by both primes. Splitting according to the first prime among \(2,3,5,7,11\) that fails to divide \(d\), and using auxiliary primes \(13\) or \(17\), forces \(d\) to be divisible by one of \(2310,2730,4290,6006,13090,15015\), each exceeding \(2025\).

full_proof.text:
Call a positive integer lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. We prove that there do not exist integers \(a\ge 2\) and \(1\le d\le 2025\) for which all 150 terms
\[
a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
are lopsided. This disproves the stated existence conjecture.

We first establish the key observation.

**Conflict lemma.** Let \(p\) and \(q\) be primes having different final decimal digits, and suppose that
\[
pq\le 150.
\]
If all the numbers \(a+id\), for \(0\le i<150\), are lopsided, then
\[
p\mid d\quad\text{or}\quad q\mid d.
\]

Indeed, suppose for contradiction that neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\). Since \(p\) and \(q\) have different final digits, they are distinct primes. Thus \(d\) is relatively prime to both \(p\) and \(q\), and hence
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Consequently, multiplication by \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\). There is therefore a residue class \(i\pmod{pq}\) satisfying
\[
id\equiv -a\pmod{pq}.
\]
Choose its least nonnegative representative. Then
\[
0\le i<pq\le 150,
\]
so \(0\le i<150\), and the congruence says
\[
pq\mid a+id.
\]
In particular, both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime divisors of \(a+id\). The number \(a+id\) is positive (in fact it is at least \(a\ge2\)), so these are genuine prime divisors of that term. But \(p\) and \(q\) have different final decimal digits, contradicting the assumption that \(a+id\) is lopsided. This proves the conflict lemma.

Now suppose, toward a contradiction, that such \(a\) and \(d\) exist. We repeatedly apply the conflict lemma. All numbers used below—
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17
\]
—are primes. Whenever the lemma is applied, the two displayed primes have different residues modulo \(10\), and their product is at most \(150\).

We split first according to whether \(2\mid d\).

### Case 1: \(2\nmid d\)

Apply the conflict lemma to each of the pairs
\[
(2,3),\quad (2,5),\quad (2,7),\quad (2,11),\quad (2,13).
\]
The final digit of \(2\) is different from the final digits \(3,5,7,1,3\) of the other primes, respectively, and the products are
\[
2\cdot3=6,
\quad 2\cdot5=10,
\quad 2\cdot7=14,
\quad 2\cdot11=22,
\quad 2\cdot13=26,
\]
all at most \(150\). Because \(2\nmid d\), the alternative supplied by the conflict lemma forces
\[
3\mid d,
\quad 5\mid d,
\quad 7\mid d,
\quad 11\mid d,
\quad 13\mid d.
\]
These are five distinct primes, hence their product divides \(d\):
\[
3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=15015\mid d.
\]
Since \(d>0\), this implies \(d\ge15015>2025\), contrary to \(d\le2025\).

It remains to consider the case \(2\mid d\).

### Case 2: \(2\mid d\) but \(3\nmid d\)

Apply the conflict lemma to
\[
(3,5),\quad (3,7),\quad (3,11),\quad (3,17).
\]
Their respective final digits are different: \(3\) differs from \(5,7,1,7\). Their products are
\[
15,\quad21,\quad33,\quad51,
\]
all at most \(150\). Since \(3\nmid d\), the lemma gives
\[
5\mid d,
\quad 7\mid d,
\quad 11\mid d,
\quad 17\mid d.
\]
Together with \(2\mid d\), and using the fact that these are distinct primes, we obtain
\[
2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot17=13090\mid d.
\]
Thus \(d\ge13090>2025\), again impossible.

We may therefore assume from now on that both \(2\mid d\) and \(3\mid d\).

### Case 3: \(2\mid d\), \(3\mid d\), but \(5\nmid d\)

Apply the conflict lemma to
\[
(5,7),\quad (5,11),\quad (5,13).
\]
The final digit \(5\) is different from \(7,1,3\), and
\[
5\cdot7=35,
\quad 5\cdot11=55,
\quad 5\cdot13=65,
\]
all at most \(150\). Since \(5\nmid d\), we conclude that
\[
7\mid d,
\quad11\mid d,
\quad13\mid d.
\]
Combining these with \(2\mid d\) and \(3\mid d\) yields
\[
2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=6006\mid d.
\]
Hence \(d\ge6006>2025\), a contradiction.

Thus we may also assume \(5\mid d\).

### Case 4: \(2\mid d\), \(3\mid d\), \(5\mid d\), but \(7\nmid d\)

Apply the conflict lemma to the pairs
\[
(7,11)\quad\text{and}\quad(7,13).
\]
Their final digits are respectively \((7,1)\) and \((7,3)\), and
\[
7\cdot11=77\le150,
\qquad
7\cdot13=91\le150.
\]
Since \(7\nmid d\), the lemma forces
\[
11\mid d\quad\text{and}\quad13\mid d.
\]
Together with \(2,3,5\mid d\), this gives
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13=4290\mid d.
\]
Therefore \(d\ge4290>2025\), again a contradiction.

We are left with
\[
2\mid d,
\quad3\mid d,
\quad5\mid d,
\quad7\mid d.
\]
There are two final subcases.

### Case 5: \(11\mid d\)

The five distinct primes \(2,3,5,7,11\) all divide \(d\), so their product divides \(d\):
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310\mid d.
\]
As \(d>0\), this gives \(d\ge2310>2025\), impossible.

### Case 6: \(11\nmid d\)

Use the conflict lemma for \(p=11\) and \(q=13\). These primes end in different digits, namely \(1\) and \(3\), and
\[
11\cdot13=143\le150.
\]
The lemma says \(11\mid d\) or \(13\mid d\). The former is excluded in this subcase, so \(13\mid d\). Therefore the five distinct primes \(2,3,5,7,13\) divide \(d\), and hence
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13=2730\mid d.
\]
It follows that \(d\ge2730>2025\), once more contradicting \(d\le2025\).

The case split is exhaustive: either \(2\nmid d\), or \(2\mid d\); in the latter event, successively either \(3\nmid d\), \(5\nmid d\), \(7\nmid d\), or all of \(2,3,5,7\) divide \(d\), after which either \(11\mid d\) or \(11\nmid d\). Every branch contradicts \(1\le d\le2025\).

For completeness, the product-divisibility steps above use the elementary fact that if distinct primes \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\) all divide an integer \(d\), then \(r_1\cdots r_k\mid d\). This follows successively from coprimality: if \(x\mid d\), \(r\mid d\), and \(\gcd(x,r)=1\), then \(xr\mid d\). Since every listed product is larger than \(2025\), no positive \(d\le2025\) can be divisible by it.

Thus no arithmetic progression of 150 terms with positive common difference at most \(2025\), beginning at an integer \(a\ge2\), can consist entirely of numbers whose prime divisors share one final decimal digit. The conjectured integers \(a\) and \(d\) do not exist.
